description: Students building FALSIFY, a tool that tries to prove its own findings wrong. It attacks each result with real NASA data and only reports what survives across separate, unrelated datasets. If the data cannot decide, it says so. Written in Python, runs offline, working now. Looking for: Data Visualization (our biggest gap), Earth Science (MODIS, VIIRS, Landsat), Statistics (trends over time), Design, Storytelling.
summary:
Synaptic is an AI research harness for NASA Earth data, with an app anyone can use. In Trend Detective, the challenge app, a user picks one of 41 NASA variables, any region and any period, and gets the time series with an honest verdict in plain words, using tests that account for year-to-year memory in climate data.

Behind it, a group of NVIDIA Nemotron agents searches NASA data for changes, but no agent can promote its own claim: every test is written down before its data are downloaded, and code runs it on data the agents never saw. Of 81 pre-registered tests, most came back “not shown”, and we report them all.

What the harness found: northern Morocco’s 2026 drought break added 17 to 21 km³ of water to the ground, confirmed by a second satellite; three trends in a NASA reference study are not detected in 24 years of MODIS; and when the UAE moved its weekend, the cleanest-air day moved with it.
details:
WHAT IT DOES Synaptic answers one question honestly: is this trend in NASA data real? It has two layers.

  1. Trend Detective (the challenge app). Anyone chooses a variable from 41 NASA datasets described in plain words (MODIS, OMI, AIRS, GPM IMERG, MERRA-2, GLDAS, GRACE/GRACE-FO, CERES), a region (any country, US state, a box or the whole world) and a period and season. The app downloads only that variable and region from NASA Earthdata Cloud, draws the yearly and monthly series and a map of where it changes, and tests significance. The verdict is written in words, for example: "No significant trend (p = 0.31). That does not prove there is no trend." Twelve series fetched through the app and through NASA Giovanni agree to better than 0.001%.
  2. The AI research harness. NVIDIA Nemotron models play a research group: a planner, a principal investigator, worker and supervisor pairs that must look at the raw numbers and charts, referees and an auditor. They explore NASA data and propose testable claims. Code decides: each confirmation test is written down and committed before its data are downloaded, the data that judge it are hidden from the agents, and a verdict can only be raised by code (referees and the auditor can only lower it). A non-significant result is reported as "not shown", never as "refuted".

WHAT IT FOUND (81 pre-registered tests, all reported)

  • Northern Morocco, winter 2025-26: the rains that ended a seven-year drought added 17 to 21 km³ of water to the ground (NASA GRACE, two independent solutions). Confirmed by a second satellite, SMAP, with a test written before its data were downloaded (p = 0.011, below a threshold of 0.0167 set in advance).
  • A NASA reference study re-tested: three river-mouth chlorophyll trends reported as significant (SeaWiFS 1998-2007) are not detected in 24 years of MODIS Aqua once year-to-year memory is accounted for (p = 0.37 to 0.43). Two separate versions of our code agree.
  • UAE weekend change, 2022: the day with the cleanest air over Dubai and Abu Dhabi moved from Friday to Sunday (NASA OMI nitrogen dioxide; none of 20,000 random reshuffles matched it). Control cities show nothing.
  • Lake Chad basin and central Sahara, 2024: the largest seasonal water gains since 2003 (about 75 km³ and 46 to 73 km³). The second-satellite check was "not shown" for Lake Chad and "supported, not confirmed" for the Sahara, and we report exactly that. We searched NASA ADS and found no published measurement of the Morocco, Lake Chad, Sahara or UAE results. We do not claim to be first.

HOW IT WORKS Statistics: Sen slope and Mann-Kendall with a correction for year-to-year carry-over, the effective number of independent years, 95% intervals, and an event-departure test; a correction for the number of tests in every registration. Every reported number is recomputed offline by one command, python -m synaptic reproduce (8 of 8 evidence bundles pass), and the code has 39 automated tests.

BENEFITS: Students, journalists, farmers and water agencies can test their own region's trend without a specialist, and get an answer that refuses to over-claim. Scientists receive only leads that passed a test written in advance. The rule "agents propose, code decides" works anywhere an independent check exists.

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE: A hosted version of the app, more NASA and partner-agency datasets, and a harness that keeps watching new NASA data and hands confirmed leads to scientists.

TOOLS: Python (NumPy, pandas, SciPy, statsmodels, xarray, netCDF4, matplotlib), Flask and vanilla JavaScript for the app, NVIDIA Nemotron models through the NVIDIA API, Kaggle GPUs, NASA Earthdata Cloud (OPeNDAP, Harmony), ArcGIS Online and StoryMaps, LaTeX for the paper.

MORE Research paper (PDF): https://0x-type.github.io/Synaptic/docs/paper/synaptic_paper.pdf ArcGIS StoryMap: https://arcg.is/1uOXai3 Code: https://github.com/0x-type/Synaptic
